title: After the row
description: The argument is rarely what damages a relationship; it is the quality of what happens in the hour after it.

body.heading: Cool down before you repair
paragraphs: Repair attempted while hearts are still pounding usually restarts the fire. Agree, if you can, on the pause itself: “I need twenty minutes, and then I want to sort this out.” The second half of that sentence is what separates a cooling-off from a walk-out.
Use the pause for its purpose — breathing, water, the deliberate rehearsal of the other person’s likely view — not for building a better prosecution.

body.heading: Return to the point, not the pile
paragraphs: When you return, take the original issue and only the original issue. Rows have a gravity that pulls in old grievances, character verdicts, and unrelated evidence; every addition makes agreement smaller. One thing, settled, beats five things aired.
Start with your own contribution, however small your share honestly is. “I raised my voice” costs little and unlocks the other person’s matching honesty with remarkable reliability.

body.heading: End with the relationship stated
paragraphs: Close the repair by saying the quiet part: “We’re okay. This mattered, and we’re okay.” People can endure hard conversations remarkably well when they are certain of the ground underneath them. State the ground.
Then let it be finished. A settled row that keeps being re-opened for sport teaches everyone to stop settling them.

takeaway: Pause on purpose, repair the one issue, own your share first, and end by stating that you are okay.
